title: Latent Denoising Makes Good Tokenizers
claim: Training the tokenizer to reconstruct clean signals from corrupted latents, using masking and interpolative noise, yields robust representations for generation.
layout: 1 panel, left-to-right pipeline, formula between encoder and decoder, legend on top
description: A single left-to-right diagram of the tokenizer training pipeline. On the left, a 4x4 grid of input patches, some light blue and some gray (masked), feeds an Encoder, drawn as a large blue rounded box. The encoder outputs a column of blue latent tokens. These are mixed with a column of colorful Gaussian-noise tiles via the formula '· (1 − τ) + τ ·', with τ ~ U(0,1). The result is a column of orange noised latents. The orange tokens are placed into a grid together with lavender mask tokens and passed to a Decoder, a second blue box. The Decoder outputs a clean light-blue target grid on the right. A legend across the top labels masked patches, Gaussian noise and mask token. Captions below read 'Masking noise' and 'Interpolative latent noise'. Blue, orange and gray make the stages easy to tell apart.
caption: Our latent denoising tokenizers (l-DeTok) framework. During tokenizer training, we randomly mask input patches (masking noise) and interpolate encoder-produced latent embeddings with Gaussian noise (interpolative latent noise). The decoder processes these deconstructed latents and mask tokens to reconstruct the original images in pixels. We refer to this process as denoising. When serving as a tokenizer for downstream generative models, both noises are disabled.
abstract: Despite their fundamental role, it remains unclear what properties could make tokenizers more effective for generative modeling. We observe that modern generative models share a conceptually similar training objective -- reconstructing clean signals from corrupted inputs, such as signals degraded by Gaussian noise or masking -- a process we term denoising. Motivated by this insight, we propose aligning tokenizer embeddings directly with the downstream denoising objective, encouraging latent embeddings that remain reconstructable even under significant corruption. To achieve this, we introduce the Latent Denoising Tokenizer (l-DeTok), a simple yet highly effective tokenizer trained to reconstruct clean images from latent embeddings corrupted via interpolative noise or random masking. Extensive experiments on class-conditioned (ImageNet 256x256 and 512x512) and text-conditioned (MSCOCO) image generation benchmarks demonstrate that our l-DeTok consistently improves generation quality across six representative generative models compared to prior tokenizers. Our findings highlight denoising as a fundamental design principle for tokenizer development, and we hope it could motivate new perspectives for future tokenizer design.
